title: Contrastive load sprint — eddychart lab notes (Indra)
summary: Quick personal log of a two-day sprint exploring mixed short/long request mixes with KV-cache priming and adaptive batching. Found a consistent p99 amplification when long requests overlap cache-miss windows; adaptive batch timeout reduced cost but increased p95 for short requests.
content:
Goal: stress a small Redwood-like serving node with a contrastive load mix: frequent short completions (8 tokens) interleaved with infrequent long generations (~512 tokens). See whether KV cache priming + adaptive timeout reduces per-token cost without breaking short-request latency SLOs.

Environment:
- Host: dedicated single A100-40GB instance (test harness sandbox)
- Runtime: local build of serving-runtime (feature/eddychart-adaptive-batch)
- Model: open-13B-quant (q4f), KV-cache enabled
- Clients: 50 worker clients (poisson arrival), orchestrated by perf-driver v0.9.
- Duration: 2 x 60m runs (baseline, then adaptive-batch-on)
- Mix: 70% short (8 tokens), 30% long (512 tokens) by request count
- Target ingress QPS: 220 steady, peak bursts to 600 for 30s every 5m

Baselines (adaptive-batch OFF):
- Steady QPS 220 (mixed):
  - short reqs: p50=12ms, p95=85ms, p99=260ms
  - long reqs: p50=320ms, p95=1.8s, p99=3.4s
  - overall tokens/s: ~18k
  - observed spike behavior: p99 for short requests spikes to 800–1200ms during long-request flushes (KV cold windows)

Hypothesis at start:
- If KV-cache priming for long reqs is enabled (warm prefix caching), and adaptive-batch-timeout is tuned lower, we can keep short p95 < 100ms while reducing average cost per token by 8–12%.

Adaptive-batch ON (timeout 6ms, max-batch 64):
- Steady QPS 220 (mixed):
  - short reqs: p50=14ms, p95=120ms, p99=340ms
  - long reqs: p50=290ms, p95=1.6s, p99=3.0s
  - tokens/s: ~20k (slightly higher due to better packing of long tokens)
  - cost proxy: CPU/GPU active duty reduced 9% over baseline (pilot accounting metric)

Key observations:
1) Short-request degradation: enabling adaptive batching with a slightly longer timeout (6ms) improved packing for long requests but caused short p95 to worsen from 85ms -> 120ms. The latency tail (p99) also increased. This is the core tension: batching packs more efficiently but adds buffer delay for short WV requests.
2) KV-cache interplay: when a long request misses KV entries (context not primed), we saw a spike cascade where multiple short requests behind the same worker experience p99 amplification. Correlation: cold KV window + large batch dispatch => spike.
3) Burst behavior: during peak bursts to 600 QPS, the node hit saturations that caused kernel-level preemption (observed in dmesg). When preemption coincided with long-request flush, tail latencies for shorts jumped to multiple seconds.
4) Throughput vs cost: adaptive batch increased tokens/sec and reduced GPU overhead; on average cost-per-token reduced by ~9% (preliminary). But user-facing SLO tradeoff was negative for latency-sensitive short completions.

Small ascii chart of short p95 across runs (minutes):
min:  5 10 15 20 25 30 35 40 45 50 55 60
base: 85 82 88 90 86 100 240 92 87 295 270 88
adpt: 120 125 118 122 130 140 420 130 126 410 390 128
(note: visible spikes at minutes 30 and 50 correspond to long-request cold windows)

Interpretation / quick heuristics:
- Adaptive batching is cost-effective when workload is dominated by long-token requests. For highly mixed workloads with latency-sensitive shorts, use adaptive-batch with per-client short-request bypass (fast-path) or much smaller max-timeouts (~1–2ms).
- KV priming matters: warm prefixes before long requests save the amplification cascade. If you schedule long requests behind a warm prefix job or pre-warm the KV segment, tails drop substantially.
- Safety valve: add short-request priority lanes — immediate dispatch for requests with token_count < 32 and a separate tiny batcher thread.

Anomalies / open puzzles:
- Why do we get 2–4s spikes only when long-request cold misses align with kernel preemption? Hypothesis: a driver-level page migration or occasional HBM swap leading to >200ms stall, which then blocks batch completions. Need kernel perf traces and nvml logs for the 30/50-min spike windows.
- Slightly higher tokens/s under adaptive batching despite worse short latency — likely because long requests pack better and amortize per-request overhead. Confirm by running long-only workloads with the same batch config.

Immediate next steps (short list):
- Re-run long-only baseline + adaptive-batch to confirm tokens/s delta and cost proxy. (assigned: Marta)
- Add a fast-path for short requests (<32 tokens) that bypasses the adaptive batcher and goes to a microbatcher with <1ms hold. Test at 220 QPS with same burst profile. (assigned: me)
- Collect kernel traces (perf, nvprof), and nvml counters for minutes 30/50 in next run. Correlate with dmesg. (assigned: Noor)
- Test aggressive KV priming: run a 5m warm-run where long request prefixes are primed every 30s and measure p99 amplification reduction. (assigned: Marta)

Notes to self:
- Avoid changing two knobs at once in future runs; separate timeout and max-batch experiments.
- Consider client-side placement: stagger long requests across workers so KV cold windows don't align.
- Record a micro video of the tail spike; it helps when explaining to SRE.

Log snippets and quick copies:
- Perf-driver seed: 20260225T10:12Z, config: mix=0.7/0.3, burstPattern=5m@30s:600, poisson-lambda calibrated for 220 mean.
- Baseline run id: run-20260225-b1; adaptive run id: run-20260225-b2.
